title: Houthi Strikes Intensify: Yemen Rebels Demonstrate Growing Power Against Saudi Arabia【AP News】
body:
The Houthi movement in Yemen has escalated its campaign against Saudi Arabia, launching a series of high‑profile attacks that have struck the kingdom’s main international gateway, King Abdullah International Airport in Jeddah, and seized strategic positions along the Red Sea’s Bab al‑Mandab strait. The unprecedented reach of the rebel force, backed by Iran, signals a widening gap in Saudi defensive capabilities and raises fresh concerns about the security of one of the world’s most vital maritime arteries.

In the past month, Houthi missiles and drones have repeatedly targeted the Jeddah airport, forcing temporary shutdowns, grounding flights, and prompting the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority to issue emergency alerts. While none of the strikes have caused casualties, the attacks have disrupted the flow of passengers and cargo, underscoring the rebels’ ability to project power hundreds of kilometres beyond Yemen’s borders. Saudi officials have downplayed the incidents, attributing them to “isolated technical failures,” but the pattern of coordinated assaults suggests a deliberate strategy to pressure the kingdom’s air‑travel hub and erode confidence in its security apparatus.

The air campaign coincides with a ground offensive that has seen Houthi forces capture several villages near the Bab al‑Mandab, the narrow choke point that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Control of this area grants the rebels a foothold over one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes, through which roughly 10 percent of global oil trade passes each day. International shipping firms have already reported heightened insurance premiums and rerouting costs as vessels adopt more cautious navigation routes to avoid potential Houthi‑laid mines and anti‑ship missiles. The move marks a significant shift from the rebels’ earlier reliance on coastal raids to a more expansive, land‑based presence that threatens both maritime and overland logistics.

Analysts attribute the Houthi surge to a confluence of factors: a steady flow of Iranian weapons, including precision‑guided missiles and long‑range drones; the waning of U.S. and coalition air support after the 2023 drawdown; and the kingdom’s preoccupation with internal security challenges, such as the aftermath of the 2022 Riyadh protests and the ongoing war in Yemen’s southern provinces. “The Houthis have been methodically building a hybrid warfare capability that blends conventional artillery, missile technology, and cyber‑enabled targeting,” said Dr. Laila Al‑Saadi, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. “Their recent successes are less about a sudden breakthrough and more about years of incremental capacity building.”

Saudi Arabia’s response has been a mix of defensive posturing and limited retaliatory strikes. The kingdom’s air force has conducted several sorties against Houthi positions in the Saada and Hajjah governorates, yet the effectiveness of these missions remains unclear. Moreover, the Saudi navy has increased patrols near the Bab al‑Mandab, deploying additional frigates and unmanned surface vessels to detect and neutralize threats. However, the sheer expanse of the Red Sea and the rebels’ ability to launch attacks from mobile launch platforms make a comprehensive seal‑off difficult. Critics argue that Saudi leadership is constrained by the political cost of a full‑scale escalation, which could draw Iran deeper into the conflict and destabilize the broader Gulf region.

The evolving Houthi threat has prompted renewed diplomatic activity. The United Nations has called for an emergency meeting of the Security Council to discuss “the escalating risk to international shipping and civilian air travel.” Meanwhile, European and Asian trade groups are lobbying for a multinational task force to secure the Red Sea corridor, echoing the multinational anti‑piracy operations that were active a decade ago. If the Houthis continue to expand their operational reach, the pressure on Saudi Arabia—and on the global supply chain—will intensify, potentially prompting a recalibration of regional security arrangements.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of the conflict will hinge on whether Saudi Arabia can restore a credible deterrent posture and secure international support for a coordinated response. Failure to do so could embolden the Houthis to launch even more ambitious attacks, possibly targeting oil terminals or critical infrastructure deeper within the kingdom. Conversely, a concerted diplomatic and military effort that curtails Iranian arms transfers and bolsters coalition capabilities may force the rebels to revert to guerrilla tactics, limiting their capacity to disrupt global trade. The coming weeks will thus be pivotal in determining whether the Red Sea remains a conduit of commerce or becomes a flashpoint of renewed great‑power rivalry.
